facts.claim: Major safe-sleep guidance prefers layered clothing or a wearable blanket (sleep sack) over loose blankets and other coverings to keep a baby warm.
Soft objects, loose bedding, pillows, quilts, comforters and bumper pads should stay out of the crib; these recommendations are for healthy babies up to 1 year of age.
A wearable blanket should be the right size for the baby and should not cover the head.
Sleep sacks that compress the arms, chest and body should stop once a baby shows signs of starting to roll over; sleep sacks that do not swaddle can be used as long as the parent wants.
Weighted sleepers, swaddles, sleep sacks and blankets are not safe for infants.
Babies need no more than one layer beyond what a comfortable adult would wear in the same room; a one-piece sleeper or sleep sack can serve as sleep clothing.
Newborn sizes are often outgrown within days, so the AAP advises buying larger sizes unless the baby is premature or very small.
The AAP advises washing new baby clothes before use because newborns tend to have sensitive skin.
Babies do not need shoes until they start walking.

In Germany, a body or undershirt plus pajamas is listed as sufficient bedtime clothing; in warm weather a thin pajama without feet or a short-sleeved body is enough, and hats should be avoided indoors and in bed.

facts.claim: US infant garments sized nine months and under must carry a size label in months of age, such as '0 to 3 mos.' or '9 mos.'.

For infant garments in the nine-months-and-under range, a one-piece garment cannot exceed 64.8 cm (25.75 in) in length, and no piece of a two-piece garment can exceed 40 cm (15.75 in); this is a regulatory eligibility limit, not a size chart.
Tight-fitting sleepwear sizes must be expressed in months or numbers, not letters such as XS, S, M, L or XL.
Babies typically gain about 1 to 1.5 inches (2.5 to 4 cm) in length each month between one and four months, so a '0-3 months' label can run out on length before weight.

facts.claim: The CPSC says loose-fitting cotton or cotton-blend garments, such as oversized T-shirts, can catch fire easily when worn as sleepwear, and recommends snug-fitting or flame-resistant sleepwear for children's sleep.

Children's sleepwear flammability rules (16 CFR parts 1615 and 1616) cover sizes 0 to 6X and 7 to 14; tight-fitting garments that meet the snug-fit sizing and labeling rules are exempt from the flammability testing but must carry the label 'WEAR SNUG-FITTING, NOT FLAME RESISTANT'.
Blanket-style sleepers and robes are covered by the children's sleepwear flammability standards; recalled blanket sleepers were found to fail those standards.
The AAP advises washing new baby clothes before use because newborns tend to have sensitive skin.
Parents should check labels for flame-resistant sleepwear and washing instructions, and avoid soap flakes, which can strip flame-retardant properties.
Babies should wear about one layer more than an adult would need in the same room, and overbundling raises overheating risk, which is linked to SIDS.
In warm weather, a thin pajama without feet or a short-sleeved body is sufficient bedtime clothing for a baby.
